texts.bands.amide.ii.chemist: Amide II (N-H bending with C-N stretching), strong, ~1515-1570 cm⁻¹; expected with amide I. Absent in tertiary amides. A single source (plus NIST). False friends: asymmetric NO₂, NH₃⁺.
texts.bands.amide.ii.counsellor: This peak comes from the combined motion of the N-H and C-N bonds of an amide. It is read together with the carbonyl peak.
texts.bands.amide.ii.teaching: Amide II arises from the coupled motion of two movements: the N-H bend and the C-N stretch. The amide C-N has some double-bond character (the same resonance that lowers amide I), so it vibrates at a high wavenumber for a single bond (~1515-1570 cm⁻¹). An N-H is needed: tertiary amides lack this band. Amide II, together with amide I, therefore separates primary and secondary amides from tertiary ones.
texts.bands.aromatic.overtones.chemist: Aromatic ring overtones and combination bands («benzene fingers»), weak, ~1650-2000 cm⁻¹; the pattern depends on the substitution. False friend: a weak amide I.
texts.bands.aromatic.overtones.counsellor: This group of small weak peaks accompanies an aromatic ring. They should not be mistaken for a weak carbonyl.
texts.bands.c_c_o.ester.arom.chemist: Asymmetric C-C-O stretching of an aromatic ester, strong, ~1250-1310 cm⁻¹; expected with conjugated C=O at ~1700-1730. A single source. False friend: aryl ether.
texts.bands.c_c_o.ester.arom.counsellor: This intense peak comes from a bond of the ester attached to a ring. It is read with the carbonyl peak.
texts.bands.c_c_o.ester.sat.chemist: Asymmetric C-C-O stretching of a saturated ester, strong, ~1160-1250 cm⁻¹ (acetates ~1230-1240, cocaine ~1265-1275); expected with C=O at ~1725-1755; rule to be used with a candidate only. A single source. False friend: alcohol C-O.
texts.bands.c_c_o.ester.sat.counsellor: This intense peak comes from a bond of the ester. It is read with the carbonyl peak.
texts.bands.c_cl.aliphatic.chemist: Aliphatic C-Cl stretching, strong, ~550-850 cm⁻¹, a very wide window; candidate only. False friends: out-of-plane C-H of benzene.
texts.bands.c_cl.aliphatic.counsellor: This intense peak, in a very crowded region, can come from a bond between carbon and chlorine. It is not enough alone.
texts.bands.c_o.alcohol.chemist: C-O stretching of alcohols and polyols, strong, ~1000-1210 cm⁻¹ (sugars 1000-1150, mannitol ~1017); expected with hydrogen-bonded O-H. False friends: esters, sulfates, silicates.
texts.bands.c_o.alcohol.counsellor: This intense, broad peak comes from the C-O bond of alcohols and sugars. Many substances have one, so it is not enough alone.
texts.bands.c_o.alcohol.teaching: The C-O bonds of alcohols and sugars are polar and absorb strongly, at ~1000-1150 cm⁻¹ for sugars. A sugar has many slightly different C-O bonds, so their bands add up in a wide, strong region, which is why mannitol, lactose and cellulose resemble each other. It falls in the same zone as sulfates, phosphates and silicates: to tell them apart the broad O-H above 3200 cm⁻¹ is sought and the minor bands are examined.
texts.bands.c_o.aryl_ether.chemist: Asymmetric C-O stretching of an aryl ether, strong and sharp, ~1200-1300 cm⁻¹ (methylenedioxy ~1244); a wide window. False friends: C-C-O of aromatic esters, aromatic C-N.
texts.bands.c_o.aryl_ether.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the bond between a ring and an oxygen (an ether on a ring). Other groups fall in the same region.
texts.bands.c_o.aryl_ether.teaching: The C-O bond between a ring and an oxygen has some double-bond character (the oxygen donates electrons to the ring) and so vibrates higher than aliphatic ethers (~1200-1300 cm⁻¹). It is intense because the bond is very polar. It falls in the fingerprint zone, where aromatic C-N and aromatic esters also fall: it is therefore read together with other bands. In methylenedioxy compounds (MDMA) the band at ~1244 is part of a triplet with ~1031 and ~930.
texts.bands.c_o.phenol.chemist: Phenol C-O stretching, strong and sharp, ~1200-1260 cm⁻¹ (paracetamol ~1224); expected with hydrogen-bonded O-H; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: aryl ether.
texts.bands.c_o.phenol.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the bond between a ring and an O-H group (phenol). It is read with the broad O-H peak.
texts.bands.c_o_c.ether.chemist: Asymmetric C-O-C stretching of an ether, strong and sharp, ~1050-1150 cm⁻¹; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: alcohol C-O.
texts.bands.c_o_c.ether.counsellor: This intense peak comes from an oxygen between two carbons (an ether). Other groups fall in the same region.
texts.bands.carbonate.oop.chemist: Out-of-plane bending of CO₃²⁻, medium and sharp, ~850-885 cm⁻¹; expected with the band at ~1400-1510. False friend: out-of-plane C-H of para-disubstituted rings.
texts.bands.carbonate.oop.counsellor: This peak comes from a carbonate, a mineral salt. It is read together with a broader peak near 1400.
texts.bands.carbonate.stretch.chemist: Asymmetric CO₃²⁻ stretching, strong and broad, ~1400-1510 cm⁻¹ (calcium carbonate, bicarbonate); expected with the band at ~850-885 and without C-H. False friend: CH₂ scissoring.
texts.bands.carbonate.stretch.counsellor: This broad, intense peak comes from a carbonate, a mineral salt, and not from an organic molecule. It is found in some cutting agents.
texts.bands.carboxylate.asym.chemist: Asymmetric COO⁻ stretching, strong and broad, ~1550-1610 cm⁻¹; expected with the symmetric stretch at ~1300-1420. False friend: asymmetric NO₂.
texts.bands.carboxylate.asym.counsellor: This broad peak comes from the carboxylate group, the charged form of an acid. It is read together with a peak lower down.
texts.bands.carboxylate.sym.chemist: Symmetric COO⁻ stretching, medium and broad, ~1300-1420 cm⁻¹; expected with the asymmetric stretch at ~1550-1610. Rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: CH₃ umbrella.
texts.bands.carboxylate.sym.counsellor: This broad peak comes from the carboxylate group, the charged form of an acid. It is read together with a peak higher up.
texts.bands.cc.alkene.chemist: Alkene C=C stretching, variable intensity, ~1620-1680 cm⁻¹; to be confirmed by =C-H at ~3010-3100. False friend: amide I.
texts.bands.cc.alkene.counsellor: This peak comes from a double bond between two carbons. It is often weak and can be confused with other nearby peaks.
texts.bands.cc.triple.chemist: C≡C stretching of an alkyne, ~2100-2260 cm⁻¹, weak; it can be absent in symmetric internal alkynes. False friends: air CO₂; salt overtones.
texts.bands.cc.triple.counsellor: This weak peak comes from a triple bond between two carbons. If the molecule is symmetric it can be absent altogether.
texts.bands.ch.aromatic.chemist: Aromatic C-H stretching, weak and sharp, ~3000-3130 cm⁻¹ (above 3000 = ring or unsaturation). False friend: vinyl C-H.
texts.bands.ch.aromatic.counsellor: This weak peak comes from the C-H bonds of a flat carbon ring. It shows a ring, not which substance it is.
texts.bands.ch.aromatic.teaching: The carbon of an aromatic ring has a slightly stiffer bond to hydrogen than a saturated carbon: in Hooke's law a larger force constant k raises the wavenumber. This is why ring C-H absorb above 3000 cm⁻¹ and those of CH₃ and CH₂ below. The band is weak because the dipole moment changes little. The 3000 cm⁻¹ boundary is a rule of thumb, not a law: some halides such as CH₂Cl₂ have saturated C-H above 3000.
texts.bands.ch.vinyl.chemist: =C-H stretching of an alkene, ~3010-3100 cm⁻¹, medium; to be confirmed by C=C at ~1620-1680. False friend: aromatic C-H.
texts.bands.ch.vinyl.counsellor: This peak comes from the C-H bond next to a carbon-carbon double bond. It is read together with the peak of the double bond.
texts.bands.ch2.rocking.chemist: CH₂ rocking in a long chain, medium, ~715-750 cm⁻¹; expected with the methylene C-H bands. Candidate only. False friend: out-of-plane C-H of monosubstituted benzene.
texts.bands.ch2.rocking.counsellor: This medium-intensity peak comes from the rocking of a chain of CH2 groups. It is found in oils and paraffins.
texts.bands.ch2.scissoring.chemist: CH₂ scissoring, medium and sharp, ~1445-1485 cm⁻¹; of little diagnostic value on its own. False friends: ring C=C ~1500, asymmetric CH₃ bend.
texts.bands.ch2.scissoring.counsellor: This peak comes from the scissoring bend of the two hydrogens of a CH2 group. Almost all molecules with chains have one.
texts.bands.ch2.scissoring.teaching: In the scissoring mode the two hydrogens of CH₂ move closer and farther apart in the plane, like the blades of scissors. It is a bending motion, not a stretching one, and bending an angle takes less energy than stretching a bond: hence it falls far below the C-H stretches (~1445-1485 cm⁻¹, against ~2900). It falls near the ring C=C (~1500) and the CH₃ bend (~1450): alone it is not enough to recognise a group.
texts.bands.ch2.stretch_asym.chemist: Asymmetric C-H stretching of a methylene group, ~2915-2936 cm⁻¹, medium and sharp; ubiquitous, of little diagnostic value on its own. Intense in oils and paraffins.
texts.bands.ch2.stretch_asym.counsellor: This peak comes from the C-H bonds of a CH2 group, found in carbon chains. It tells little about which substance is present.
texts.bands.ch2.stretch_asym.teaching: CH₂ has two C-H bonds moving together: in the symmetric mode they lengthen and shorten together (~2850 cm⁻¹), in the asymmetric mode one lengthens while the other shortens (~2925 cm⁻¹). CH₂ chains are abundant in oils, waxes and paraffins and give intense peaks precisely because many identical groups absorb at the same frequency. A sample with many CH₂ therefore shows two tall, sharp peaks below 3000 cm⁻¹ that can mask the rest.
texts.bands.ch2.stretch_sym.chemist: Symmetric C-H stretching of a methylene group, ~2845-2865 cm⁻¹, medium and sharp. False friend: symmetric CH₃ stretching.
texts.bands.ch2.stretch_sym.counsellor: This peak comes from the C-H bonds of a CH2 group moving together. It tells little about which substance is present.
texts.bands.ch3.bend_asym.chemist: Asymmetric CH₃ bend, medium, ~1430-1470 cm⁻¹, overlapping the CH₂ scissoring; rule to be used with a candidate only.
texts.bands.ch3.bend_asym.counsellor: This peak comes from the bending of the C-H bonds of a methyl group. Almost all organic molecules have one.
texts.bands.ch3.stretch_asym.chemist: Asymmetric C-H stretching of a methyl group, ~2950-2975 cm⁻¹, medium and sharp; of little diagnostic value on its own.
texts.bands.ch3.stretch_asym.counsellor: This peak comes from the C-H bonds of a methyl group (CH3). Almost all organic molecules have one, so it tells little.
texts.bands.ch3.stretch_asym.teaching: In a CH₃ group the three C-H bonds move together in different ways: in the symmetric mode they all lengthen together (~2870 cm⁻¹), in the asymmetric mode one shortens while the others lengthen (~2960 cm⁻¹). The asymmetric mode has the higher wavenumber because it deforms the structure more. Almost every organic molecule has a CH₃, so this peak is almost always present and says little alone: it tells that an aliphatic part exists, not which substance it is.
texts.bands.ch3.stretch_sym.chemist: Symmetric C-H stretching of a methyl group, ~2860-2885 cm⁻¹, medium and sharp. False friend: symmetric CH₂ stretching.
texts.bands.ch3.stretch_sym.counsellor: This peak comes from the C-H bonds of a methyl group (CH3) moving together. Almost all organic molecules have one.
texts.bands.ch3.umbrella.chemist: Symmetric CH₃ bend (umbrella), medium, ~1365-1385 cm⁻¹. False friend: symmetric NO₂.
texts.bands.ch3.umbrella.counsellor: This peak comes from the «umbrella» bend of a methyl group. Almost all organic molecules have one.
texts.bands.cho.fermi.chemist: Aldehyde C-H stretching, a Fermi-resonance doublet, ~2695-2830 cm⁻¹; the peak at ~2720 is the most isolated. False friends: N-CH₃ and the salt «comb».
texts.bands.cho.fermi.counsellor: This peak, often double, comes from the C-H bond of an aldehyde. It can be confused with the peaks of amine salts.
texts.bands.cn.aliphatic_amine.chemist: Aliphatic amine C-N stretching, weak, ~1020-1250 cm⁻¹, in a crowded region; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: alcohol C-O.
texts.bands.cn.aliphatic_amine.counsellor: This weak peak comes from the bond between a carbon and a nitrogen. It falls in a crowded region.
texts.bands.cn.aromatic_amine.chemist: Aromatic amine C-N stretching, medium, ~1250-1360 cm⁻¹; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: aryl ether.
texts.bands.cn.aromatic_amine.counsellor: This medium-intensity peak comes from the bond between a ring and a nitrogen. Other groups fall in the same region.
texts.bands.cn.imine.chemist: Imine C=N stretching, medium, ~1590-1690 cm⁻¹, a wide window overlapping C=C and amide I. False friends: amide I, C=C.
texts.bands.cn.imine.counsellor: This peak comes from a double bond between carbon and nitrogen. Other groups fall in the same region.
texts.bands.cn.nitrile.chemist: C≡N stretching of a nitrile, ~2210-2280 cm⁻¹, sharp; intensity varies between sources, do not use it as a criterion. False friends: air CO₂; salt overtones.
texts.bands.cn.nitrile.counsellor: This sharp peak comes from a triple bond between carbon and nitrogen. It falls in an almost empty region of the spectrum.
texts.bands.co.acid.chemist: Carboxylic acid (dimer) C=O stretching, strong, ~1680-1730 cm⁻¹; expected with very broad O-H at ~2500-3300 and O-H wag at ~900-960. False friends: conjugated ester, saturated ketone.
texts.bands.co.acid.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbonyl of an acid. It is read together with the broad O-H peak of the acid.
texts.bands.co.aldehyde.chemist: Aldehyde C=O stretching, strong and sharp, ~1685-1740 cm⁻¹; expected with the C-H doublet at ~2695-2830. False friend: saturated ester.
texts.bands.co.aldehyde.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbonyl of an aldehyde. It is read together with its characteristic C-H peaks.
texts.bands.co.amide.chemist: Amide C=O stretching (amide I), strong, ~1630-1690 cm⁻¹ (fentanyls, caffeine, lidocaine, paracetamol, synthetic cannabinoids); lower than ketones. False friends: water bending, aryl ketone, C=C.
texts.bands.co.amide.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbonyl of an amide, a group in many molecules. Other groups fall nearby: alone it is not enough.
texts.bands.co.amide.teaching: In the amide the nitrogen lone pair spreads onto the carbonyl (resonance): the C=O has less double-bond character and a lower k, so it falls lower than ketones (~1630-1690 cm⁻¹). This band is called amide I. It is intense because the C=O has a large dipole moment. Tertiary amides, such as fentanyls, lack the N-H and therefore lack amide II as well. Caffeine, lidocaine and paracetamol also have bands nearby: they are told apart by their other bands.
texts.bands.co.aryl_ketone.chemist: Aryl ketone (cathinones) C=O stretching, strong and sharp, ~1660-1700 cm⁻¹; the window is wide because polymorphs fall at different positions. False friends: amides, caffeine, lidocaine.
texts.bands.co.aryl_ketone.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbonyl of a ketone attached to a ring. Other groups fall nearby, so it is not enough alone.
texts.bands.co.aryl_ketone.teaching: In cathinones the C=O is attached to an aromatic ring. Conjugation moves electrons toward the carbonyl and softens the double bond: the force constant k falls and so does the wavenumber (~1660-1700 cm⁻¹, against ~1700-1725 for a saturated ketone). The peak is intense and sharp. Two polymorphs of the same salt can fall at different positions because the surroundings in the crystal change the strength of the bond, hence the wide window. Position alone is not enough: amides and caffeine fall nearby.
texts.bands.co.ester.conj.chemist: Conjugated ester (benzoate) C=O stretching, strong and sharp, ~1700-1730 cm⁻¹; expected with aromatic C-C-O at ~1250-1310. False friends: saturated ketone, carboxylic acid.
texts.bands.co.ester.conj.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbonyl of an ester attached to a ring. It falls a little lower than that of an ordinary ester.
texts.bands.co.ester.conj.teaching: When the ester C=O is attached to an aromatic ring (benzoate), the ring electrons also spread onto the carbonyl group: the double bond loses some of its character and becomes less stiff. With a lower k, Hooke's law gives a lower wavenumber: ~1700-1730 cm⁻¹ instead of ~1725-1755. This is why in cocaine the two carbonyl peaks are attributed one to the saturated methyl ester (higher), the other to the conjugated benzoate. The difference is small: resolution matters.
texts.bands.co.ester.sat.chemist: Saturated ester C=O stretching, strong and sharp, ~1725-1755 cm⁻¹ (opiate acetates, the methyl ester of cocaine). Expected with C-C-O at ~1160-1250. False friends: aldehyde, saturated ketone.
texts.bands.co.ester.sat.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbon-oxygen double bond of an ester. Esters are common: on its own it does not indicate the substance.
texts.bands.co.ester.sat.teaching: C=O is a stiff double bond between light atoms: in Hooke's law a high force constant k gives a high wavenumber (~1700-1750 cm⁻¹). It is very intense because the dipole moment changes a lot during the motion: it is often the tallest peak of the spectrum. In the saturated ester the neighbouring oxygen draws some density from the carbon and stiffens the C=O, so it falls higher (~1725-1755) than the ketone. In ATR strong bands move down by a few cm⁻¹ compared with transmission.
texts.bands.co.imide.chemist: Imide C=O stretching, strong multi-component band, ~1670-1790 cm⁻¹ (examples: barbiturates, xanthines); expected with imide N-H at ~3100-3270. A single independent source. False friend: saturated ester.
texts.bands.co.imide.counsellor: This peak or group of peaks comes from the carbonyls of an imide, a group with two neighbouring C=O. It is read with its N-H.
texts.bands.co.ketone.sat.chemist: Saturated ketone C=O stretching (for example cyclohexanone), strong and sharp, ~1700-1725 cm⁻¹; higher than conjugated ketones. False friends: conjugated ester, carboxylic acid.
texts.bands.co.ketone.sat.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the carbonyl of a ketone. On its own it does not say which substance is present.
texts.bands.co.ketone.sat.teaching: In the ketone the C=O is bonded only to two carbons. There is no oxygen to stiffen the bond and no ring to soften it: the wavenumber falls in the reference zone of the carbonyl (~1700-1725 cm⁻¹). If the carbonyl is conjugated with a ring (aryl ketone) it goes down, if it sits in a very small ring it goes up. The peak is intense because the dipole moment changes a lot. Ketamine, for example, has a ketone in a six-membered ring, not conjugated, and falls higher than cathinones.
texts.bands.co2.artifact.chemist: Asymmetric stretching of atmospheric CO₂ (doublet ~2340/2360), ~2280-2400 cm⁻¹: a background artefact, to be masked or ignored and flagged if intense. It is not a band of the sample.
texts.bands.co2.artifact.counsellor: This peak does not come from the sample but from the carbon dioxide in the air. It can change between background and measurement.
texts.bands.co2.artifact.teaching: The carbon dioxide in the air absorbs strongly near 2350 cm⁻¹ and at ~667. The instrument subtracts the background, but if the amount of CO₂ changes between the background and the measurement, a peak remains (possibly pointing downward) that does not belong to the sample. It is therefore recognised by its position and its doublet shape, and should be ignored or masked; if it is very intense it is better to repeat the background. It falls in a region where samples barely absorb, except nitriles and alkynes.
texts.bands.co2.artifact_bend.chemist: O=C=O bending of atmospheric CO₂, ~660-675 cm⁻¹, sharp, accompanies the band at ~2340/2360: a background artefact, not a band of the sample.
texts.bands.co2.artifact_bend.counsellor: This sharp peak does not come from the sample but from the carbon dioxide in the air, like the one near 2350.
texts.bands.h2o.bend.chemist: H-O-H bending of adsorbed or crystal water, ~1610-1650 cm⁻¹, broad; expected with O-H stretching at ~3300-3500. False friends: amide I, NH₂ scissoring.
texts.bands.h2o.bend.counsellor: This broad peak can come from water held by the sample. It does not say which substance is present.
texts.bands.h2o.stretch.chemist: O-H stretching of adsorbed or crystal water, ~3300-3500 cm⁻¹, broad; expected with the H-O-H bend at ~1610-1650. A frequent contaminant of hygroscopic salts; false friend: hydrogen-bonded O-H.
texts.bands.h2o.stretch.counsellor: This broad peak can come from water held by the sample. It does not indicate the substance, but water changes the look of the spectrum.
texts.bands.nch3.stretch.chemist: Symmetric C-H stretching of N-CH₃, ~2765-2825 cm⁻¹, medium; expected for amines as free bases, the rule is excluded when the N-H⁺ envelope is present. False friends: O-CH₃ and aldehyde C-H.
texts.bands.nch3.stretch.counsellor: This peak comes from the methyl group attached to a nitrogen. It is seen mainly when the nitrogen is not in salt form.
texts.bands.nh.amide.chemist: Amide N-H stretching, ~3170-3370 cm⁻¹, medium; to be confirmed by amide I (~1630-1690) and amide II. False friend: hydrogen-bonded O-H.
texts.bands.nh.amide.counsellor: This peak comes from the N-H bond of an amide. It is read with the carbonyl peaks; alone it does not indicate the substance.
texts.bands.nh.amide.teaching: The N-H bond vibrates at high wavenumbers because it involves a light hydrogen, but less so than O-H: the bond is less stiff. In amides, hydrogen bonds between molecules lower the band and broaden it a little. The band is, however, narrower than O-H, which helps to tell them apart. One band means one N-H (secondary amide), two bands mean two N-H (primary amide). It is never assigned alone: amide I, the C=O near 1650 cm⁻¹, and amide II are looked for as well.
texts.bands.nh.amine1.chemist: N-H stretching of a primary amine (free base): two bands, asymmetric and symmetric, ~3250-3510 cm⁻¹, medium and narrower than O-H. False friend: hydrogen-bonded O-H.
texts.bands.nh.amine1.counsellor: This peak, often double, comes from the N-H bonds of an NH2 group. On its own it does not say which substance is present.
texts.bands.nh.amine2.chemist: N-H stretching of a secondary amine (free base), one weak band, ~3280-3400 cm⁻¹; it may not be visible in a mixture. False friend: amide N-H.
texts.bands.nh.amine2.counsellor: This weak peak comes from the N-H bond of an amine with a single hydrogen on the nitrogen. In a mixture it can vanish.
texts.bands.nh.imide.chemist: Imide N-H stretching, ~3100-3270 cm⁻¹, medium; hydrogen bonding in the solid lowers it strongly compared to the gas phase. Expected with imide C=O. False friend: amide N-H.
texts.bands.nh.imide.counsellor: This peak comes from the N-H bond of an imide, a group with two neighbouring C=O. It is read with the carbonyl peaks.
texts.bands.nh.indole.chemist: N-H stretching of an indole or non-alkylated heterocycle, ~3380-3490 cm⁻¹, sharp; in solids hydrogen bonding lowers it. No open source for solid indole: rule to be confirmed on reference spectra.
texts.bands.nh.indole.counsellor: This sharp peak comes from the N-H bond of a ring containing nitrogen. On its own it does not say which substance is present.
texts.bands.nh2.scissoring.chemist: NH₂ scissoring of a primary amine, medium and broad, ~1560-1650 cm⁻¹; expected with the two N-H bands at ~3250-3510. False friends: water, amide I.
texts.bands.nh2.scissoring.counsellor: This broad peak comes from the scissoring motion of an NH2 group. It is read together with the N-H peaks higher up.
texts.bands.nh2plus.bend.chemist: NH₂⁺ bend of a secondary amine salt, one weak band, ~1560-1620 cm⁻¹; expected with the N-H⁺ envelope. A single source. False friend: ring ~1600.
texts.bands.nh2plus.bend.counsellor: This weak peak comes from the bending of a group with a positive charge on the nitrogen. It is found in secondary amine salts.
texts.bands.nh2plus.stretch.chemist: N-H⁺ stretching of a secondary amine salt (methamphetamine, MDMA, N-methyl cathinones), very broad envelope ~2200-3100 cm⁻¹ with sub-bands; sources disagree on the low end, hence the wide window. False friends: acid O-H; tertiary N-H⁺.
texts.bands.nh2plus.stretch.counsellor: This very broad peak comes from a salt where the nitrogen carries two hydrogens. It depends on the salt form and occurs in many substances.
texts.bands.nh2plus.stretch.teaching: In salts the nitrogen carries a positive charge and a hydrogen that forms a strong hydrogen bond with the anion (for example chloride). A hydrogen bond this strong lowers the wavenumber by hundreds of cm⁻¹ and spreads it over a wide range: hence the band is a very broad envelope, with sub-bands from overtones and combinations. One hydrogen more or less on the nitrogen moves the centre of the envelope, but sources disagree on the limits, hence the wide window. The envelope says «salt», not which amine.
texts.bands.nh3plus.bend.chemist: NH₃⁺ bends of a primary amine salt, weak, often two, ~1500-1625 cm⁻¹; expected with the N-H⁺ envelope at ~2800-3200. False friends: ring ~1600, amide II.
texts.bands.nh3plus.bend.counsellor: These weak peaks, often two, come from the bending of a group with a positive charge on nitrogen, in primary amine salts.
texts.bands.nh3plus.stretch.chemist: N-H⁺ stretching of a primary amine salt (for example amphetamine), very broad envelope ~2800-3200 cm⁻¹ with overlapping C-H; expected with two NH₃⁺ bends. False friend: acid O-H.
texts.bands.nh3plus.stretch.counsellor: This very broad peak comes from a salt where the nitrogen carries three hydrogens. The salt form produces it, not the free base.
texts.bands.nhplus.combination.chemist: Series of overtones and combination bands of amine salts, weak, ~2000-2800 cm⁻¹ (a «comb»); not to be assigned to C≡C or C≡N.
texts.bands.nhplus.combination.counsellor: These weak, closely spaced peaks accompany the broad peak of amine salts. They should not be mistaken for other groups.
texts.bands.nhplus.stretch.chemist: N-H⁺ stretching of a tertiary amine salt (for example cocaine hydrochloride), very broad envelope ~2300-2700 cm⁻¹; it distinguishes the salt from the free base, which lacks it. False friend: secondary N-H⁺.
texts.bands.nhplus.stretch.counsellor: This very broad peak comes from a salt in which the nitrogen carries a single hydrogen. It says a salt is present, not which one.
texts.bands.nhplus.stretch.teaching: In the salt of a tertiary amine a single hydrogen remains on the nitrogen, bonded to the anion through a very strong hydrogen bond. The stronger the bond, the lower the wavenumber: the envelope therefore tends to fall lower (~2300-2700 cm⁻¹) than that of salts of amines with more hydrogens. On going from salt to free base this envelope disappears, which is why it tells the salt form from the base. It is broad because each molecule in the crystal has a slightly different hydrogen bond.
texts.bands.nitrate.stretch.chemist: Asymmetric NO₃⁻ stretching, strong and broad, ~1340-1400 cm⁻¹. False friend: symmetric NO₂ of nitro compounds.
texts.bands.nitrate.stretch.counsellor: This broad, intense peak comes from a nitrate, a mineral salt. It is found in some salts and cutting agents.
texts.bands.no2.stretch_asym.chemist: Asymmetric NO₂ stretching, strong, ~1485-1560 cm⁻¹ (5-nitro nitazenes); expected with the symmetric stretch at ~1290-1390. False friends: amide II, carboxylate.
texts.bands.no2.stretch_asym.counsellor: This intense peak comes from a nitro group (a nitrogen with two oxygens). It is read together with a second peak of the group.
texts.bands.no2.stretch_sym.chemist: Symmetric NO₂ stretching, strong, ~1290-1390 cm⁻¹; expected with the asymmetric stretch at ~1485-1560. False friends: CH₃ umbrella, inorganic nitrate.
texts.bands.no2.stretch_sym.counsellor: This intense peak comes from a nitro group (a nitrogen with two oxygens). It is read together with a second peak of the group.
texts.bands.o_c_c.ester.chemist: O-C-C stretching of an ester, strong, ~1030-1130 cm⁻¹ (cocaine ~1105); expected with C=O at ~1700-1755; rule to be used with a candidate only. A single source. False friend: alcohol C-O.
texts.bands.o_c_c.ester.counsellor: This intense peak comes from another bond of the ester, low in the spectrum. It is read with the carbonyl peak.
texts.bands.o_ch2_o.c_o.chemist: C-O stretching of O-CH₂-O, medium, ~1030-1055 cm⁻¹; expected with the aryl ether at ~1244 and the ring band at ~930 (the triplet together, never one band alone). False friend: alcohol C-O.
texts.bands.o_ch2_o.c_o.counsellor: This peak comes from a ring with two oxygens joined by a CH2 (methylenedioxy). It is not enough alone: the set of three peaks matters.
texts.bands.o_ch2_o.ring.chemist: Methylenedioxy ring band (O-CH₂-O bending), medium, ~915-950 cm⁻¹ (~930); expected with the aryl ether at ~1244 and C-O at ~1031. False friend: acid O-H wag.
texts.bands.o_ch2_o.ring.counsellor: This peak comes from a ring with two oxygens joined by a CH2 (methylenedioxy). It is not enough alone: the set of three peaks matters.
texts.bands.och3.stretch.chemist: Symmetric C-H stretching of O-CH₃ (methoxy), ~2810-2850 cm⁻¹, medium and sharp. False friends: N-CH₃ and aldehyde C-H.
texts.bands.och3.stretch.counsellor: This peak comes from the methyl group attached to an oxygen (methoxy). It helps to recognise certain molecules but can be confused with nearby peaks.
texts.bands.oh.acid.chemist: O-H stretching of the carboxylic acid dimer, very broad, ~2500-3300 cm⁻¹, often without a maximum and overlapping the C-H bands. Expected together with C=O at ~1680-1730. False friend: the N-H⁺ envelope of amine salts.
texts.bands.oh.acid.counsellor: This very broad peak comes from the O-H of an acid and covers nearby peaks. On its own it does not indicate the substance.
texts.bands.oh.acid_wag.chemist: Out-of-plane O-H wag of the carboxylic acid (dimer), medium and broad, ~900-960 cm⁻¹; expected with C=O at ~1680-1730 and O-H at ~2500-3300; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: methylenedioxy ring band.
texts.bands.oh.acid_wag.counsellor: This broad peak comes from the out-of-plane motion of the O-H of an acid. It is read together with the peaks of the acid.
texts.bands.oh.free.chemist: Free (non-hydrogen-bonded) O-H stretching, sharp, ~3580-3650 cm⁻¹; compatible with a hindered or isolated OH, rare in solids. False friend: the talc OH (~3675).
texts.bands.oh.free.counsellor: This peak comes from an O-H group not bonded to its neighbours. Rare in solids; alone it does not indicate the substance.
texts.bands.oh.hbonded.chemist: Hydrogen-bonded O-H stretching, strong and very broad, ~3200-3570 cm⁻¹; compatible with alcohols, phenols, sugars, water. False friends: adsorbed water; N-H of amides and amines (narrower).
texts.bands.oh.hbonded.counsellor: This broad peak comes from O-H groups bonded together (hydrogen bonding), as in alcohols, sugars or water. Alone it does not indicate the substance.
texts.bands.oh.hbonded.teaching: Hydrogen is very light, so in Hooke's law (ν̃ = √(k/μ) / 2πc) the reduced mass μ is small and O-H vibrates at high wavenumbers. When molecules bond to each other through hydrogen bonds, each feels a slightly different surrounding: the band moves down and broadens, because many slightly different versions of the same vibration add up. It is intense because the dipole moment changes a lot during the motion. This is why water and sugars give a wide «hill» rather than a peak. In ATR, bands above 2500 cm⁻¹ look weaker.
texts.bands.oop.124.chemist: Out-of-plane C-H of 1,2,4-trisubstituted benzene, strong, ~790-900 cm⁻¹; a single source (LibreTexts, reproducing Sigma-Aldrich), literature only until verified on spectra. Candidate only. False friends: para-disubstituted, carbonate.
texts.bands.oop.124.counsellor: These intense peaks come from the out-of-plane bending of the C-H bonds of a ring with three substituents. They are not enough alone.
texts.bands.oop.meta.chemist: Out-of-plane C-H of meta-disubstituted benzene, strong and sharp, ~750-810 cm⁻¹; the third band falls at ~690 or ~880 depending on the source. Candidate only. False friend: monosubstituted.
texts.bands.oop.meta.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the out-of-plane bending of ring C-H bonds when two substituents sit in a middle position. Alone it is not enough.
texts.bands.oop.mono.chemist: Out-of-plane C-H of monosubstituted benzene, strong and sharp, ~710-770 cm⁻¹; expected with the ring band at ~680-710. Candidate only. False friends: ortho- and meta-disubstituted.
texts.bands.oop.mono.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the out-of-plane bending of ring C-H bonds when the ring has one substituent. Read it with a peak near 700.
texts.bands.oop.mono.teaching: In out-of-plane bending the ring hydrogens oscillate above and below the plane. Five adjacent hydrogens (a monosubstituted ring) vibrate together and give a strong band near 700-770 cm⁻¹, accompanied by the ring bend at ~680-710. With fewer adjacent hydrogens, or with isolated hydrogens, the band moves: the pattern of out-of-plane bands therefore tells how the ring is substituted. But in a mixture these bands blur with those of the cutting agents.
texts.bands.oop.ortho.chemist: Out-of-plane C-H of ortho-disubstituted benzene, strong and sharp, ~735-770 cm⁻¹ (ketamine ~772); candidate only. False friend: monosubstituted.
texts.bands.oop.ortho.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the out-of-plane bending of the C-H bonds of a ring with two neighbouring substituents. It is not enough alone.
texts.bands.oop.para.chemist: Out-of-plane C-H of para-disubstituted benzene, strong and sharp, ~790-860 cm⁻¹ (4-MMC ~833); candidate only. False friend: 1,2,4-trisubstituted.
texts.bands.oop.para.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the out-of-plane bending of the C-H bonds of a ring with two opposite substituents. It is not enough alone.
texts.bands.phosphate.stretch.chemist: Asymmetric PO₄³⁻ stretching, strong and very broad, ~1000-1100 cm⁻¹ (dicalcium phosphate). False friends: sulfate, silicate.
texts.bands.phosphate.stretch.counsellor: This very broad, intense peak comes from a phosphate, a mineral salt. It is found in some cutting agents.
texts.bands.ring.c_c_1500.chemist: Aromatic ring C=C stretching, variable intensity, ~1440-1515 cm⁻¹; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friend: CH₂ scissoring.
texts.bands.ring.c_c_1500.counsellor: This peak comes from the motion of the bonds of the aromatic ring. It shows a ring, not which substance it is.
texts.bands.ring.c_c_1600.chemist: Aromatic ring C=C stretching, variable intensity, ~1580-1620 cm⁻¹; rule to be used with a candidate only. False friends: NH₂⁺ bend, C=N.
texts.bands.ring.c_c_1600.counsellor: This peak comes from the motion of the bonds of the aromatic ring. It shows a ring, not which substance it is.
texts.bands.ring.c_c_1600.teaching: In the aromatic ring the six carbon-carbon bonds are neither single nor double: they have an intermediate character, and the ring vibrates as a whole. The ring stretching vibrations appear as a pair of bands near 1600 and 1500 cm⁻¹ (~1580-1620 and ~1440-1515). The intensity varies a lot with the substituents. These bands tell that a ring exists but do not identify it.
texts.bands.ring.mono_bend.chemist: Ring bend of monosubstituted benzene, strong and sharp, ~680-710 cm⁻¹; expected with the out-of-plane band at ~710-770. Candidate only. False friend: sulfate bending.
texts.bands.ring.mono_bend.counsellor: This intense peak comes from the ring bending of a benzene with a single substituent. It is read with a peak just above.
texts.bands.silicate.si_o.chemist: Asymmetric Si-O stretching, strong and very broad, ~950-1200 cm⁻¹ (talc ~1018 in KBr, ~973 in ATR: a strong shift). Expected with Mg-OH at ~3675. False friends: alcohol C-O, sulfate.
texts.bands.silicate.si_o.counsellor: This very broad, intense peak comes from a silicate, a mineral such as talc. It is found in some cutting agents.
texts.bands.sulfate.bend.chemist: SO₄²⁻ bending, medium, often a doublet, ~600-680 cm⁻¹; expected with the stretch at ~1040-1145.
texts.bands.sulfate.bend.counsellor: These medium-intensity peaks come from a sulfate, a mineral salt. They are read together with the broad peak near 1100.
texts.bands.sulfate.stretch.chemist: Asymmetric SO₄²⁻ stretching, strong and very broad, ~1040-1145 cm⁻¹ (amphetamine sulfate ~1050); expected with the bend at ~600-680; excluded when strong aliphatic C-H is present. False friends: alcohol and sugar C-O, phosphate, silicate.
texts.bands.sulfate.stretch.counsellor: This very broad, intense peak comes from a sulfate, a mineral salt. It is found in some salt forms and in some cutting agents.
texts.bands.sulfate.stretch.teaching: The sulfate ion has four oxygens around the sulfur and a high symmetry: its asymmetric stretch is very intense, because the charge moves a lot during the motion, and broad, because in the solid each ion feels a slightly different surrounding. It falls at ~1040-1145 cm⁻¹, where sugar C-O, phosphates and silicates also fall. In amphetamine sulfate it is the dominant band. In an organic sample it is recognised by its broad shape and the absence of strong C-H bands.
texts.bands.talc.oh.chemist: Mg-OH stretching of talc, sharp, ~3670-3685 cm⁻¹; expected with the broad Si-O band at ~950-1200. False friend: free O-H.
texts.bands.talc.oh.counsellor: This sharp peak comes from an O-H group inside a layered mineral. On its own it is not enough.
texts.modes.bend_in_plane.definition: The angle between bonds changes in the plane; used when the literature does not say whether it is scissoring or rocking.
texts.modes.combination.definition: A weak band near the sum of the frequencies of two fundamental vibrations.
texts.modes.lattice.definition: Vibration of an ion (carbonate, sulfate) or of the crystal; typical of inorganic cutting agents.
texts.modes.oop.definition: A ring hydrogen moves above and below the plane of the ring; it is strong between 900 and 675 cm⁻¹ and the pattern depends on how the ring is substituted.
texts.modes.overtone.definition: A weak band near a multiple of the frequency of a fundamental vibration (due to anharmonicity).
texts.modes.ring_breathing.definition: All the bonds of the ring lengthen together: the ring swells and shrinks.
texts.modes.rocking.definition: The group swings in the plane like a pendulum and the angle between the bonds stays the same.
texts.modes.scissoring.definition: The angle between two bonds opens and closes in the plane, like scissors.
texts.modes.stretch.definition: The bond lengthens and shortens along its direction, like a spring.
texts.modes.stretch_asym.definition: Two equal bonds move oppositely: one lengthens while the other shortens.
texts.modes.stretch_sym.definition: Two equal bonds lengthen and shorten together.
texts.modes.twisting.definition: The two atoms move out of the plane on opposite sides, as in a twist.
texts.modes.wagging.definition: The two atoms move out of the plane together on the same side, like a wagging tail.
texts.regions.carbonyl.name: Carbonyls (C=O)
texts.regions.carbonyl.short: Esters, ketones, acids, amides: the most intense and useful bands.
texts.regions.ch_bend.name: C-H bending and ionic groups
texts.regions.ch_bend.short: CH₂ scissoring, CH₃, symmetric NO₂, carbonate.
texts.regions.ch_stretch.name: C-H stretching
texts.regions.ch_stretch.short: Above 3000 rings and double bonds, below 3000 CH₃ and CH₂.
texts.regions.double_bonds.name: Double bonds and N-H bending
texts.regions.double_bonds.short: Ring C=C, C=N, amide II, NO₂, water.
texts.regions.far.name: Heavy atoms and lattice
texts.regions.far.short: C-Br, C-I, inorganic ions; noise from the diamond and the detector.
texts.regions.instrument.name: Instrument zone
texts.regions.instrument.short: Diamond absorption and air CO₂; only rare triple bonds (C≡N, C≡C) appear here.
texts.regions.oop.name: Out-of-plane bending (fingerprint)
texts.regions.oop.short: C-H of aromatic rings: they tell how the ring is substituted.
texts.regions.salt_nh.name: Amine salts (N-H⁺) and special C-H
texts.regions.salt_nh.short: Broad envelope of amine salts; O-CH₃, N-CH₃ and aldehyde C-H between 2850 and 2700.
texts.regions.single_bonds.name: C-O and C-N single bonds (fingerprint)
texts.regions.single_bonds.short: Esters, ethers, alcohols, amines; sulfates, phosphates, silicates: a crowded zone.
texts.regions.xh_stretch.name: O-H and N-H stretching
texts.regions.xh_stretch.short: Broad when hydrogen-bonded (alcohols, sugars, water); two sharp bands for NH₂.
texts.substance_bands.4_cmc.hydrochloride.840: Band at ~840 cm-1: out-of-plane bend of the para-disubstituted ring, expected for 4-CMC hydrochloride.
texts.substance_bands.4_mmc.hydrochloride.1686: Band at ~1686 cm-1: aryl-ketone C=O, typical of cathinones; it falls near caffeine, lidocaine and amides.
texts.substance_bands.4_mmc.hydrochloride.833: Band at ~833 cm-1: out-of-plane bend of the para-disubstituted ring; a hint of the 4-substituted isomer, only with a candidate.
texts.substance_bands.amphetamine.sulfate_race: Band at ~1049 cm-1: sulfate stretch, very intense and broad; it tells the sulfate from the hydrochloride.
texts.substance_bands.caffeine.anhydrous.1212: Band at ~1212 cm-1: C–N stretching of the caffeine xanthine rings (pyrimidinedione and imidazole); not an ether.
texts.substance_bands.caffeine.anhydrous.1692: Band at ~1692 cm-1: first of the two coupled C=O of caffeine (the other is at ~1645); in a mixture it may move by 5-10 cm-1.
texts.substance_bands.caffeine.anhydrous.744: Band at ~744 cm-1: very intense and isolated, the most useful to recognise caffeine in a mixture.
texts.substance_bands.cellulose.microcrystalli: Band at ~1029 cm-1: group of strong broad C-O bands, typical of polysaccharides; it does not tell cellulose from sugars.
texts.substance_bands.cocaine.base.1734: Band at ~1734 cm-1: C=O of the methyl ester in the base form; in the hydrochloride it is at ~1728.
texts.substance_bands.cocaine.base.712: Band at ~712 cm-1: out-of-plane bend of the monosubstituted ring, compatible with the base form (in the salt it is at ~729).
texts.substance_bands.cocaine.hydrochloride.17: Band at ~1712 cm-1: C=O of the benzoate (conjugated ester); with ~1728 it makes the doublet typical of tropane esters.
Band at ~1728 cm-1: C=O of the methyl ester, expected for cocaine hydrochloride together with the band at ~1712.
texts.substance_bands.cocaine.hydrochloride.72: Band at ~729 cm-1: out-of-plane bend of the monosubstituted ring; in the free base it falls lower, at ~712.
texts.substance_bands.ketamine.hydrochloride.1: Band at ~1720 cm-1: C=O of the cyclohexanone, higher than that of cathinones (~1686); the free base is at ~1699.
texts.substance_bands.ketamine.hydrochloride.7: Band at ~772 cm-1: the strongest, out-of-plane bend of the ortho-disubstituted ring.
texts.substance_bands.levamisole.hydrochloride: Band at ~1529 cm-1, broad: C=N stretch of the protonated amidine; to be confirmed, no open source with its bands was found.
texts.substance_bands.mdma.hydrochloride.1244: Band at ~1244 cm-1: aryl-alkyl C-O-C of the methylenedioxy group; alone it is not enough, the triplet with ~1032 and ~930 counts.
texts.substance_bands.mdma.hydrochloride.930: Band at ~930 cm-1: mode of the dioxole ring O-CH2-O; in street samples it may fall at ~922.
texts.substance_bands.paracetamol.solid.1224: Band at ~1224 cm-1: phenol C-O stretch, strong; together with ~1651 and ~835 it is compatible with paracetamol.
texts.substance_bands.phenacetin.solid.1241: Band at ~1241 cm-1: aryl-ethyl C-O-C, strong; with ~1047 it tells phenacetin from paracetamol.
texts.substance_bands.thca_a.free_acid.1612: Band at ~1612 cm-1: C=O of the acid held by an internal hydrogen bond; for this reason it is not looked for at ~1700.
